title: Parkinsonism as an initial presentation of Creutzfeldt‐Jakob disease: A case report and review of literature
case_prompt:
A 69-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of progressive gait disturbance. Soon after onset, her family noted a symmetrical hand tremor, slowness of movement, and frequent falls. One month later, she described a subjective “chilling” sensation inside her body. She then developed personality changes, persecutory delusions, and unprovoked fear. Over the following months, her gait worsened, necessitating a walking aid, tremors intensified in both hands and her chin, and generalized myoclonic jerks appeared.

Her medical history was notable for breast cancer treated with lumpectomy, chemoradiotherapy, and tamoxifen two years earlier, with no evidence of recurrence.

On examination, she was awake and alert but disoriented to time and place. Her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 13/30. There was symmetrical rigidity and bradykinesia in all limbs, a resting tremor of the hands and chin, and a stooped posture with short-stepping gait and occasional freezing. Deep tendon reflexes were 1+ to 2+ symmetrically; plantar responses were flexor. Sensory examination was unremarkable, although she reported distal paresthesia in her upper limbs. Frontal release signs included a grasp reflex, utilization behavior, and a positive Myerson sign.

Laboratory studies, including electrolytes, liver and kidney function tests, vitamin B12, thyroid function tests, and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody, were normal. Tests for systemic vasculitis were negative. Paraneoplastic and autoimmune antibodies in blood and CSF were negative. CSF analysis showed no white blood cells, a protein level of 39 mg/dL, normal glucose, and was positive for 14-3-3 protein.

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the caudate nuclei, putamina, and medial thalami, with corresponding diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC sequences. Cortical ribboning was noted in the parieto-occipital and medial frontal regions on DWI. EEG revealed nonspecific generalized slowing without periodic sharp waves.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. The combination of rapidly progressive dementia, extrapyramidal features, myoclonus, positive CSF 14-3-3 protein, and characteristic MRI findings supported sCJD — “She had typical clinical features (i.e., dementia, extrapyramidal features, myoclonus, akinetic mutism) with a disease duration of fewer than 2 years, positive 14-3-3 assay, and typical MRI features.”  
2. Alzheimer’s disease was considered but excluded because AD “typically progresses more slowly and lacks the prominent extrapyramidal signs, myoclonus, and visual disturbances seen in CJD.”  
3. Dementia with Lewy bodies was considered but deemed unlikely as DLB “usually has a more gradual onset,” despite shared features of dementia and parkinsonism.  
4. Frontotemporal dementia was considered but excluded because FTD “progresses more slowly and lacks prominent extrapyramidal features.”  
5. Corticobasal degeneration was considered but excluded since CBD “also progresses more gradually” than observed in this patient.  
6. Paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalopathy was considered given her cancer history but was ruled out as “paraneoplastic and autoimmune antibodies in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were assessed, which showed no positive result.”  
7. Central nervous system vasculitis was considered but excluded because “Tests for systemic vasculitis were all negative.”  
8. An autoimmune steroid-responsive disorder was considered; however, “a therapeutic trial of corticosteroid with 1000 mg methylprednisolone in 5 successive days was initiated. Still, no change was detected in the patient's condition.”
